description: Hello! SPX145 is a small team from Antalya, Türkiye: one student developer and a mentor. The team builds a simulation about surviving beyond Earth: in Moon Base Commander, players run a base on the Moon or Mars and balance power, water, oxygen, food and radiation protection. The student developer designed the rules, tested every mission and made the presentations; the mentor checked the science and the rules. New members in Antalya are welcome!
summary: Moon Base Commander is a 3D web game in which students run a base on the Moon or Mars for 30 days. I designed the rules, tested every mission and fixed the bugs; the team is from Antalya, Türkiye. Players choose a real landing site, align solar panels, drill ice, filter it into water, split water into oxygen, grow food, build and drive a rover, launch a relay satellite and survive emergencies such as air leaks, solar flares and Martian dust storms. Every choice has a cost in power, weight, water or time. This answers the challenge by turning engineering trade-offs into decisions a young learner can feel instead of just reading about them. It matters because future crews will face these same problems when they build outposts on the Moon and Mars, and because it teaches real NASA science in a fun way. It runs in any web browser with no installation, in English and Turkish.
details:
Moon Base Commander leads the way for future plans like building bases on the Moon and Mars. It is a junior astronaut mission trainer that runs in any web browser: 3D, no installation, works offline, in English and Turkish. Four astronauts must survive 30 days.

HOW IT WORKS

1) Choose a real landing site on a 3D globe. Each site is rated for sunlight, ice, safe ground, radiation, Earth contact and temperature. Moon: Shackleton Rim, Cabeus, Sea of Tranquility, Marius lava tube, Tycho. Mars: North Polar Ice Cap, Arcadia Planitia, Jezero, Gale, Valles Marineris.

2) Complete ten missions that unlock each other: align the solar panels, set up the greenhouse, design and drive a rover (300 kg limit), search for ice, drill it, melt and filter it in six steps, build a radiation shield, collect rock samples (five precious stones on Mars) and launch a relay satellite (orbit choice and the rocket equation).

3) Everything is connected. Power runs every machine, ice becomes water, water becomes oxygen and grows food. Players switch machines on and off to match power production and use, especially at night.

4) Survive emergencies. On the Moon: micrometeoroid leaks, solar flares and the 15-day night. On Mars: dust storms near the equator come with about 10 hours of warning; crew caught outside get hurt and need treatment, and dusty solar panels must be cleaned. Mars also has a weaker link to Earth because of its atmosphere, but no micrometeoroid leaks.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Students learn how life support, power, water, food and radiation shielding depend on each other, and they practice making trade-offs the way mission engineers do. Water and electricity matter most, and the rover has many uses, so players learn to plan ahead. The game is free and runs on ordinary school computers. Next steps: saving progress, a teacher mode with difficulty levels, making oxygen from Mars air like MOXIE, and classroom multiplayer.

TOOLS

HTML, CSS and JavaScript; Three.js for the 3D graphics; Node.js for an automated balance test that plays all 10 sites (a player who does nothing always loses, a player who plays well always survives 30 days). The code was written with the help of Claude (Anthropic AI). I turned the ideas in my mind into the game: I designed the rules (for example the Mars dust storms, the weaker Earth link and the five Mars gems), tested every mission, found the mistakes and checked the fixes.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

The same base works on two worlds with different rules, every mission is a small engineering puzzle, and the places in the game are real places NASA has explored or plans to explore. The game pauses during alarms so young players always have time to think.

Source code: https://github.com/cemyurtlak/moon-base-commander
dataRefs: Artemis III candidate landing regions near the lunar South Pole
LCROSS: water ice found in Cabeus crater (2009)
Gateway near-rectilinear halo orbit (NRHO) for the relay satellite
Fission Surface Power: nuclear power for Moon and Mars bases
MOXIE: making oxygen from Mars air
Curiosity rover (Gale Crater and Mount Sharp site, Mars minerals)
InSight lander: dust on solar panels ended the mission
Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter: orbital relay and Mars ice data
projectRefs: Nunito and Exo 2 fonts via Fontsource (SIL Open Font License)
Subsurface Water Ice Mapping (SWIM) project: buried ice at Arcadia Planitia
Claude (Anthropic): AI coding assistant used to write the game code
